---
title: "A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty"
description: "Priors are chosen on the log-odds scale and interpreted as vague. Pushed through the inverse logit, a wide Normal prior puts most of its mass on probabilities of essentially 0 or essentially 1."
date: 2026-08-11
categories:

"Weakly informative" is a claim about what a prior implies, and the log-odds
scale is not where that claim can be checked. A coefficient prior of
`Normal(0, 10)` looks generous — ten units of log-odds either way, why would
that constrain anything.

Push it through the inverse logit and it becomes a different statement: *a one
standard-deviation change in this predictor almost certainly moves the outcome
from near-impossible to near-certain.* That is not vague. It is a strong and
usually wrong belief, held accidentally.

The check takes about fifteen lines.

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng = np.random.default_rng(20260812)
N_DRAWS = 60_000

def inv_logit(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))
```

## The implied prior on a probability

Take a predictor standardised to unit variance and a baseline log-odds of zero,
so the model is `p = inv_logit(beta * x)`. Evaluating at `x = 1` — a
one-standard-deviation change, an ordinary amount of movement — the prior on
`beta` induces a prior on `p`.

```{python}
#| label: draw-priors
prior_sds = {"Normal(0, 1)": 1.0, "Normal(0, 2.5)": 2.5, "Normal(0, 10)": 10.0}

implied = {
    name: inv_logit(rng.normal(0.0, sd, N_DRAWS))
    for name, sd in prior_sds.items()
}
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-implied
#| fig-cap: "Implied prior on the outcome probability at a one-SD change in the predictor. A genuinely uninformative prior would be roughly flat across this range."
colors = {"Normal(0, 1)": "#0f766e", "Normal(0, 2.5)": "#b45309", "Normal(0, 10)": "#6d28d9"}

fig = go.Figure()
for name, draws in implied.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Histogram(
        x=draws,
        name=name,
        nbinsx=60,
        histnorm="probability density",
        opacity=0.55,
        marker_color=colors[name],
        hovertemplate="p ≈ %{x:.2f}<br>density %{y:.2f}<extra>" + name + "</extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    barmode="overlay",
    xaxis_title="implied probability of the outcome",
    yaxis_title="prior density",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.12, x=0),
    margin=dict(l=50, r=20, t=40, b=50),
    height=420,
    template="simple_white",
)
fig.show()
```

`Normal(0, 10)` is the U-shaped one. It does not spread belief across
probabilities — it concentrates it at the two extremes and leaves the middle,
where nearly every real effect lives, almost empty.

## How much mass sits at the extremes

```{python}
#| label: tbl-extremes
rows = []
for name, draws in implied.items():
    rows.append({
        "prior on β": name,
        "P(p < 0.01)": np.mean(draws < 0.01),
        "P(p > 0.99)": np.mean(draws > 0.99),
        "P(0.2 < p < 0.8)": np.mean((draws > 0.2) & (draws < 0.8)),
    })

pd.DataFrame(rows).style.format({
    "P(p < 0.01)": "{:.1%}",
    "P(p > 0.99)": "{:.1%}",
    "P(0.2 < p < 0.8)": "{:.1%}",
}).hide(axis="index")
```

Under `Normal(0, 10)`, roughly two thirds of the prior mass says the outcome is
practically determined, and only a small slice allows a moderate probability.
Under `Normal(0, 1)` most of the mass is in the moderate range, which is what
"weakly informative" is supposed to mean.

## The same problem on the risk-difference scale

Coefficients are rarely what a reader wants; the change in probability is. So
put an ordinary prior on the intercept as well and look at what the model
believes about the effect *size* before seeing any data.

```{python}
#| label: fig-risk-difference
#| fig-cap: "Implied prior on the absolute change in probability from x = 0 to x = 1. Interactive — drag to zoom, double-click to reset."
alpha = rng.normal(0.0, 1.5, N_DRAWS)

fig2 = go.Figure()
for name, sd in prior_sds.items():
    beta = rng.normal(0.0, sd, N_DRAWS)
    risk_diff = np.abs(inv_logit(alpha + beta) - inv_logit(alpha))
    fig2.add_trace(go.Violin(
        x=risk_diff,
        name=name,
        line_color=colors[name],
        orientation="h",
        side="positive",
        points=False,
        meanline_visible=True,
        hovertemplate="|Δp| ≈ %{x:.2f}<extra>" + name + "</extra>",
    ))

fig2.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="absolute change in probability, |Δp|",
    showlegend=False,
    margin=dict(l=120, r=20, t=30, b=50),
    height=380,
    template="simple_white",
)
fig2.show()
```

The wide prior's median belief is that the predictor swings the outcome
probability by most of its available range. Stated in words, nobody would
assert that. Stated as `Normal(0, 10)`, people assert it routinely.

## What this does not show

- The predictor is standardised. On an unstandardised predictor the same prior
  means something else entirely, which is a separate reason wide priors on raw
  covariates go wrong.
- With enough data the likelihood dominates and the prior stops mattering much.
  The argument here is about the small-and-sparse case — rare outcomes,
  interactions, hierarchical terms with few groups — where it does not.
- Nothing here says `Normal(0, 1)` is correct. It says the check should be run
  on the scale you actually have beliefs about, and then the prior chosen.
